\chapter{Reading — Instructions, a Form, and a First Paragraph}
\label{ch:fr-premiere-lecture}
\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read a French instruction, a line off a form, and a whole paragraph, without translating word by word.}

Sixty-three words of French in a row with no new word in them, including the sentence that admits it did not follow everything and carries on anyway.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(reading)]{(reading) — six things you would be told}

\label{lesson:FR-C45-instructions}



\begin{quote}
Every line below you have heard and said. Not one is new.

What is new is that nobody says them first.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
Parle ! Écoute ! On y va ! Un peu Beaucoup Merci
\end{quote}

Read down the list once, without stopping.

Again, and notice that three of them end in an exclamation mark and three do not. French puts a space before it, which English does not.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Parle !} and \textbf{Écoute !} are the same verbs you conjugate, with the ending taken off and nothing put in its place. That is the whole imperative.

An instruction you can only recognise by ear is one somebody has to say to you. On a page it waits, which is why a classroom is the first place a beginner reads rather than listens.

Six lines, and half of them are one word.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the six lines, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many of the six were new? (\textbf{None.})

What does French put before an exclamation mark? (\textbf{A space.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(reading)]{(reading) — six lines off a form}

\label{lesson:FR-C45-details}



\begin{quote}
The last lesson gave you things somebody says. These are things somebody writes down.

Nothing here is new.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
Nom : Marie Âge : vingt ans Lundi : le travail Mardi : un livre Une heure Dix minutes
\end{quote}

Read down once, without stopping.

Again — and notice the colon. French puts a space before that too, and the space is the clearest signal on the page that a label has ended.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{culture}
A form is the first thing a beginner can read end to end. It puts the label before the value every time, and it never asks for a verb.

That is why the last two lines are the hardest, not the first four. \textbf{Une heure} and \textbf{Dix minutes} have no label in front of them, so nothing tells you what they are for until you have read them.

Six lines, and four of them do half your work.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the six lines, once, in order, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two lines have no label? (\textbf{Une heure} and \textbf{Dix minutes}.)

What does French put before a colon? (\textbf{A space.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(reading)]{(reading) — the first paragraph}

\label{lesson:FR-C45-premiere-lecture}



\begin{quote}
Six instructions, then six lines off a form. Now a whole paragraph.

Sixty-three words, and not one of them is new.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Marie. J'habite à Paris. J'ai un frère et une sœur. Je bois du café et je mange du pain. Le jour, je vais au travail. Je travaille beaucoup, mais j'aime ça. Le soir, je lis un livre. Le livre est très bon. Je ne comprends pas tout, mais ça va. Demain, je vais parler français. Merci et au revoir.
\end{quote}

Read it once without stopping. Do not translate as you go — let the sentences arrive.

Now read it again, and notice how little work it took.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{culture}
Look at what is holding it together, because it is not vocabulary.

\textbf{Et} adds. \textbf{Mais} holds two true things apart, and it does it twice here — once about work and once about understanding. Each of those was a chapter, and none of them is longer than four letters.

Notice the tenth line especially. \textbf{Je ne comprends pas tout, mais ça va.} Somebody has admitted they did not follow everything, and the paragraph carries on. That is the most useful sentence on this page.

This is the first whole paragraph the book has asked you to hold at once, and it works because everything in it was paid for.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the paragraph aloud, once, without stopping
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many words in that paragraph were new? (\textbf{None.})

Which word appears twice and turns the sentence both times? (\textbf{Mais.})
\end{tcolorbox}
